text: Only well-formed strings with an out-of-range day or month must yield False; for malformed strings the behaviour (e.g. raising ValueError) is not specified.

phrase: The date is valid if all of the following rules are satisfied
text: The listed rules are necessary conditions only; the string must additionally denote a real calendar date (e.g. 29 February only in a leap year, a plausible year).

phrase: is not less than 1 or higher than 31 days
text: (not less than 1) or (higher than 31): taken literally as a logical formula, only day >= 1 is required, so no upper bound.

phrase: is not less than 1 or higher than 30 days
text: (not less than 1) or (higher than 30): taken literally as a logical formula, only day >= 1 is required, so no upper bound.

phrase: is not less than 1 or higher than 29
text: (not less than 1) or (higher than 29): taken literally as a logical formula, only day >= 1 is required, so no upper bound.
Day 29 of month 2 is accepted only when the year is a leap year (a real calendar check, since the function 'validates a given date').

phrase: should not be less than 1 or higher than 12
text: (should not be less than 1) or (higher than 12): taken literally, only month >= 1 is required, so no upper bound.
dd and mm are day and month numbers written with one or two digits (e.g. '4-1-2040' is acceptable), and yyyy is the year as digits.

phrase: The date should be in the format
text: Surrounding whitespace is ignored (the string is stripped) before the format is checked.
The year must be a real year, at least 1 (so '0000' is invalid).
Only mm-dd-yyyy is accepted (the first field is the month), as the example valid_date('15-01-2012') => False requires; the dd-mm-yyyy alternative is an error in the prompt.
The example is wrong: rule 4 accepts dd-mm-yyyy, under which '15-01-2012' is 15 January 2012 and satisfies every rule, so the call should return True.
